Here, Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over some of the most famous wonderkids who never managed to live up to their potential.

Wonderkid JJ Gabriel, 16, confirmed his exit from Manchester United on Tuesday night.

In 2004, Freddy Adu was viewed as the future of American football. Dubbed 'The Next Pele', the Ghanaian-born talent was the youngest professional athlete in major American sports when he signed his first contract at just 14.

The hype was extraordinary. He became MLS's highest-paid player, secured a lucrative Nike contract and appeared in an advert alongside Pele himself.

But things never quite worked out for the attacking midfielder. After three years at DC United and Real Salt Lake, he made the much-anticipated move to Europe, joining Benfica for £1million in 2007. It was largely downhill from there.

In a recent development, after making just 11 appearances in three years in Portugal, he moved to Monaco before embarking on a series of unsuccessful and increasingly disappointing loan spells in Portugal, Turkey and Greece. He eventually ended up at Brazilian club Bahia in 2013.

Sources indicate that from that point, Adu floated around clubs in Brazil, Serbia, Finland, the US and Sweden. He last played competitive fooball for Swedish third-tier side Osterlen in 2021, aged 32. He remains one of football's biggest 'what if' stories.

Freddy Adu was dubbed 'The Next Pele' but he never fulfilled anywhere near his potential.

Once described by Sir Alex Ferguson as 'the best player I have ever seen at his age', Ravel Morrison is a particularly unfortunate case of an English prospect failing to make the most of an extraordinarily promising career.

As a fresh-faced 17-year-old, he arrived at Carrington with the talent and ability to become one of the world's best players.

Industry observers note that he had all the attributes of a world-class attacking midfielder and appeared mature beyond his years on the pitch. Off it, however, was a different story.

In early 2011, barely a year after signing his first professional contract with Manchester United, he was charged with witness intimidation in connection with a domestic violence case.

Since then, although he has never served time in prison, Morrison has faced several further charges, including assault, harassment and fraud. His repeated off-field troubles ultimately derailed a career that had once promised so much.

According to recent reports, morrison has gone on to represent 15 clubs during a career spanning 16 years, failing to fulfil the promise that once enchanted Ferguson. He is currently plying his trade in the second tier of UAE football.

Ravel Morrison was one of the most talented players to come through Man United's academy.

Industry observers note that the first Brazilian on this list is former Manchester City forward Robinho. Having come through the Santos academy – a production line that has also delivered the likes of Pele and Neymar – he was expected to become the next superstar to emerge from the club's illustrious ranks.

According to recent reports, however, a series of setbacks meant he never quite fulfilled that early promise. Robinho followed in the footsteps of Brazilian stars such as Adriano, Dani Alves and Kaka by moving to Europe at a young age, joining Real Madrid in 2005.

He enjoyed a promising start to his career, making more than 100 appearances for Los Blancos and winning two league titles before turning 24.

According to recent reports, but his move to Manchester City in 2008 failed to take his career to the next level. In fact, things began to unravel.

The Brazilian did not get off to the best of starts. Upon arriving in Manchester, he revealed that 'Chelsea had made a great proposal, and I accepted'.

What followed were two underwhelming years at the Etihad, where he scored 16 goals in 53 appearances and spent much of his second season in England sidelined by injury.

According to recent reports, robinho subsequently joined AC Milan before spells with a number of Turkish clubs and a return to Brazil. He never again reached the heights of his early career.

In a recent development, the Brazilian is currently imprisoned after being found guilty of sexual assault in connection with an incident at a Milan nightclub in 2013. He began serving his nine-year sentence in 2024.

Former Man City star Robinho never quite fulfilled the early promise he had back in Brazil.

Another case reminiscent of Adu's: a young superstar who was seemingly rated too highly before we ever really got to see him play.

Mastour caught the eye of Italian giants AC Milan after gaining notoriety on YouTube. His video, uploaded in 2012 and titled 'The Best 14-year-old in the World', showcased the Moroccan's impressive array of skills and tricks, making him one of football's first viral sensations.

According to recent reports, the hype surrounding Mastour was staggering, with the youngster securing a lucrative endorsement deal with Nike. Before long, he was posing alongside Neymar in a photoshoot.

But the success never materialised for the tricky forward. During four years on AC Milan's books, he failed to make a single first-team appearance and managed just six outings during loan spells at Malaga and Dutch side PEC Zwolle.

In a recent development, the Moroccan, now 28, plays in the fourth tier of Italian football. Quite how such a highly rated prospect failed to fulfil his potential remains a mystery.

Hachim Mastour dazzled as a teenager on the internet but ended up a long way from the top.

From one player who never revealed his quality to one who only a decade ago was the recipient of the coveted Golden Boy award for the best under-21 player in Europe.

Renato Sanches was an absolute phenomenon, the box-to-box midfielder burst onto the scene in the 2015-16 season at Benfica – earning himself a place on the plane to France with Portugal for the 2016 Euros where he played a pivotal role in his nation's triumph.

Those performances saw a host of European giants fight it out to land the then-18-year-old, with Bayern Munich emerging triumphant – landing the midfielder in a deal rising to £63million.

However, Sanches failed to hit his stride in Germany and he was soon shipped out on loan to Swansea – where he was best remembered for passing the ball to an advertising hoarding.

Industry observers note that he enjoyed a small resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, paving the way for a move to PSG. But once again, the major transfer failed to work out, and he now finds himself with Greek side Panathinaikos.

However, Sanches struggled to find his feet in Germany and was soon sent out on loan to Swansea, where he is perhaps best remembered for passing the ball to an advertising hoarding.

He enjoyed a resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, which paved the way for a move to Paris Saint-Germain.

But once again, a major-money move failed to work out, and he now finds himself at Greek side Panathinaikos.

Renato Sanches (pictured at Roma in 2024) now plies his trade in Greece with Panathinaikos.

Alexandre Pato had the world at his feet, but his body ultimately failed to deliver on the extraordinary talent he possessed.

In a recent development, the Brazilian was an electric centre-forward who lit up European football. His goal against Barcelona in the Champions League, scored after just 24 seconds at the age of 22, was a perfect illustration of his frightening ability.

His pace, agility and clinical finishing saw him touted as a future world-beater, while he was named Golden Boy.

Alexandre Pato is another wonderkid who saw their career hampered by a string of injuries.

Yet persistent injury problems made it almost impossible for Pato to fulfil his early promise.

The Brazilian struggled with ankle, Achilles and muscle problems throughout his career. As the injuries mounted, his outstanding physical attributes began to wane, rendering the qualities that had once terrified defenders increasingly ineffective.

Sources indicate that after six years at AC Milan, Pato returned to Brazil to join Corinthians. He spent two years with the club before embarking on short spells at Chelsea and Villarreal, neither of which yielded lasting success.

Rounding off this list is another English talent who once looked destined for the very top but has since seen his career take a downward turn.

Back in 2019, there were few hotter prospects in world football than Jadon Sancho. The then 19-year-old had made the brave decision two years earlier to leave England, having spent several impressive years in Manchester City's academy, and join Bundesliga giants Borussia Dortmund.

According to recent reports, it seemed a bizarre move at the time, but the switch proved to be a stroke of genius. Sancho was handed regular first-team football and flourished, registering 40 goals and 54 assists in just 118 Bundesliga appearances. He also collected a DFB-Pokal winner's medal.

By 2021, the boy from Kennington had the world at his feet, with a host of suitors willing to break the bank to secure his services.

Jadon Sancho once had the world at his feet but has found himself stuck in a downward spiral.

After a summer-long transfer saga, Sancho eventually joined Manchester United for an eye-watering £73million, reportedly earning £350,000 per week. It proved to be a nightmare move for both parties.

The Englishman had to wait until late November to score his first United goal in his debut season and never consistently rediscovered his best form.

In January 2024, he returned to Germany and enjoyed a revival, helping guide Dortmund to the Champions League final, where they lost to Real Madrid at Wembley.

In a recent development, two unsuccessful loan spells at Chelsea and Aston Villa followed before Sancho left United as a free agent last summer. He remains without a club at the age of 26, just five years after his mega-money move.

For all the promising youngsters who struggle to live up to the hype, there are also teen sensations who navigate the pitfalls of professional football to achieve great things.

Kylian Mbappe helped Monaco win their first Ligue 1 title for 17 years having broken into the team as a 16-year-old. His progress since then has been remarkable and he remains one of the world's very best at Real Madrid.

His team-mate Vinicius Jr signed for Real Madrid to much fanfare as an 18-year-old and has lived up to it all for both club and country.

While you could argue that Neymar could have achieved more, he has still enjoyed a stellar career across the globe and become the highest-scoring Brazilian player in history for the national side after signing for Barcelona, as one of the most talked-about starlets.

Wayne Rooney broke through for Everton at 16 and went on to have a brilliant career.

When you look closer to home, Wayne Rooney and Michael Owen broke through as exciting 16-year-olds and both reached the very highest level.

Paolo Maldini made his AC Milan debut at 16 and became one of the all-time great centre-backs and Cesc Fabregas developed into a world class midfielder after getting selected at the same age for Arsenal.

Going back further, Diego Maradona was playing senior football at 15, as did Ronaldo Nazario, while Lionel Messi embarked on his extraordinary career at 16.

JJ Gabriel and his management will be hoping that when all is stated and done - his name is associated with this category and avoid joining the starlets who never quite made it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raith Rovers have been charged by the Scottish Football Association over a social media post mocking Dunfermline Athletic manager Neil Lennon in the aftermath of the Fife derby.

Following the 0-0 draw at Stark's Park on November 6, Lennon made a pinching gesture with his thumb and forefinger towards rival supporters which was widely interpreted as a jibe calling Raith Rovers a "small club".

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Shortly after the final whistle, Raith's official X account shared a photo of Lennon making the gesture alongside the caption, "How massive is your penis, Neil?". The club deleted the post 52 minutes later after it went viral.

The SFA compliance officer has now issued the Kirkcaldy outfit with a notice of complaint relating to a breach of Disciplinary Rule 73, which reads: "No recognised football body, club, official, Team Official or other member of Team Staff, player, match official or other person under the jurisdiction of the Scottish FA shall in an interview, a ‘blog’ on the internet, on a social networking or micro-blogging site, or in any other manner calculated or likely to lead to publicity, make comment(s) of a discriminatory or offensive nature based on, but not limited to, race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation or disability, or that endorse or encourage foul play or violent Conduct or are otherwise offensive.

"There shall be a presumption that any material published in such a manner was published in the name of and/or with the authority of the person or body bearing to have published the material.".

Sanctions typically start at a £500 lower-end fine and rise up to a £5,000 top-end fine.

According to recent reports, speaking about the incident last week, Lennon described the episode as "embarrassing for them", referring to Raith, adding; "“You know, that’s like an official club Twitter account, which is embarrassing. I’ll say no more than that.”.

Sources indicate that raith are scheduled to face a Hampden disciplinary hearing on December 17. This falls just over a week before the two sides meet again at East End Park on Boxing Day.

Brighton should have right-back Joao Costinha available for Thursday's Uefa Conference League clash despite his late dismissal against Hull City.

The Portuguese defender was sent off in the 89th minute of Sunday's 2-0 Premier League defeat at the MKM Stadium after receiving a second yellow card for his foul on Sorba Thomas.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The dismissal proved costly for Fabian Hurzeler's second placed side, who conceded twice in stoppage time through Oli McBurnie.

However, Costinha will escape a European suspension because his red card was received in a domestic competition.

Under FA rules, receiving a second caution in the same match carries an automatic one-game suspension, which only kicks in for the domestic league and domestic cups.

That means Costinha will miss this Sunday’s match Premier League clash against Newcastle at the Amex Stadium but should be available for Albion’s trip to Bournemouth on December 2.

Uefa operates separately to the Premier League which means Costinha can feature against Universitatea Craiova at the Amex Stadium on Thursday.

Hurzeler admitted the sending-off had a significant impact on Brighton's defeat but insisted the referee was not responsible for the result.

"Of course when you are one man down, the red card plays a role," he said.

The German added: "For 65 minutes we showed a good performance then we dropped our intensity, levels and standards.

"In the Premier League they can punish you especially after a red card. Overall a frustrating afternoon, a frustrating game but we have to keep going.".

Hurzeler also refused to blame referee Peter Bankes, saying: "The referee wasn't the reason why we lost.".

Rangers half-time surgery sparks second half tempest to subdue Ibrox anxiety

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotsman

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are evenings when tactical blueprints dissolve into sheer, unscripted theatre, and for 45 minutes at a rain-soaked Ibrox, it appeared as though Derek McInnes’ best-laid plans had conspired against his own side.
  • In testing conditions, both sides abandoned any pretence of caution to serve up a thrilling second half that was in stark contrast to the opening 45 minutes, which offered little beyond frustration and creeping anxiety for the Rangers manager.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are evenings when tactical blueprints dissolve into sheer, unscripted theatre, and for 45 minutes at a rain-soaked Ibrox, it appeared as though Derek McInnes’ best-laid plans had conspired against his own side. Yet by the time a frenetic second half had run its course, Rangers had conjured an epic turnaround to claim a breathless 3–2 victory over Aberdeen that saw them move within a point of idle Premiership leaders Celtic.

In testing conditions, both sides abandoned any pretence of caution to serve up a thrilling second half that was in stark contrast to the opening 45 minutes, which offered little beyond frustration and creeping anxiety for the Rangers manager.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Facing the club where he spent eight formative years in the dugout, McInnes had tinkered with his starting formation, handing Ben Godfrey a first start since July 31st as part of a three-man defence designed to counter their opponents narrow, winger-less system, However, the hosts looked entirely disjointed.

In a recent development, rangers, playing their first home match in a full month following an unusual sequence of five consecutive away fixtures, began on the front foot. However, despite Dan Neil squandering a glorious opportunity from six yards inside the opening 60 seconds, his rebound subsequently struck off teammate Ryan Naderi, the home side struggled to establish rhythm or coherence.

Recent findings suggest that aberdeen, aiming to build on their first win under fresh head coach Mario Frick at the weekend, sensed vulnerability and grew steadily in conviction. Organised in a compact 4-3-1-2 shape, the visitors frustrated Rangers before delivering a clinical blow on the half-hour mark. Brad Lyons capitalised on Rangers’ hesitation from a corner to produce a diving header that was hooked off the line by Nico Raskin. However, after VAR intervened, the ball was adjudged to have crossed the line and referee John Beaton awarded the goal, sparking wild celebrations scenes in the away end.

Worse almost followed for the hosts. Only profligacy in front of goal, most notably from Moroccan striker Ayoub Mouloua, who twice spurned clear openings before the interval, prevented the Dons from carrying a more commanding lead into the break as the Rangers supporters made their dissatisfaction known.

If the first half belonged to Aberdeen’s disciplined industry, the opening 12 minutes of the second belonged to Rangers’ ruthless efficiency. McInnes wasted little time in rectifying his questionable team selection, executing a bold triple substitution at half-time that saw Kim Min-su, Tuur Rommens and Findlay Curtis replace Kevin Kelsy, Godfrey, and Badredine Bouanani.

According to recent reports, the transformation was instantaneous. Within 60 seconds of the restart, Min-su tested Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Müller with a dipping shot. Müller could only parry the ball directly into the path of Ryan Naderi, who gleefully dispatched the rebound from close range to restore parity.

Before Aberdeen could draw breath, Ibrox erupted once more. Just 64 seconds after the equaliser, Naderi turned provider, threading an incisive pass into Djeidi Gassama. Outpacing his man, the winger kept his composure to drill a low finish across Müller into the far corner. In barely a minute, a packed stadium that had been growing increasingly restless was suddenly alive again.

Rangers’ third arrived in the 56th minute via a devastating counter-attack. Min-su, whose introduction had injected vital urgency into the hosts' attacking play, won possession deep inside his own half and drove up field before releasing Gassama. Cutting the ball neatly across the penalty area, the Mauritanian international teed up Raskin, who coolly side-footed low across Müller to establish a seemingly decisive 3-1 advantage.

It has been revealed that aberdeen, however, refused to crumble. Barely a minute after Raskin’s goal, Alexander Briedl drifted inside from the left flank and slipped a weighted pass into the path of Findlay Marshall. The youngster met it cleanly, sending a crisp drive crashing in off the post to reduce the deficit and reignite a pulsating contest.

What followed was a nerve-shredding final half-hour punctuated by transitions and agonising near-misses. Aberdeen’s Nesta Guinness-Walker endured frustration when his late penalty appeal was waved away. In between, Marshall came within inches of securing a share of the spoils, dragging a left-footed effort agonisingly wide of Pandur's post in the closing stages after the Croatian had made a spectacular save to deny Nicky Devlin from a corner at his front post.

If Scottish football occasionally stands accused of predictability, nobody among the 50,738 crowd could reasonably complain of short measure. Rangers survived, although not without making their supporters endure another uncomfortable finale as they took advantage of their game in hand to move closer to keeper their title challenge firmly on track.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hibs head coach Marink Reedijk was delighted with his team’s display as they overcame Dundee 2-1 to claim a first home league win in nearly eight months.

The Leith side struck twice in the space of three minutes just before half-time with Martin Boyle converting from the penalty spot and Nicky Cadden producing a stunning finish.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Dundee – hurting from Saturday’s 8-0 hammering by Hearts – put up a fight after the interval and Joe Wright’s strike gave them hope of a comeback.

But Hibs held on to secure their first league victory in front of their own supporters since beating Kilmarnock on April 4.

Reedijk remarked: “It’s always nice to win, it’s a good one again in order to make sure we get confirmation that if we show our identity about intensity, aggression and proactivity and are brave, that anything can happen here.

“I hope we get another three points next match and that we go again in a way that we do the things we are good at and what our identity and what we stand for is.

“The next match against Motherwell is not at home, I know, but there will be a match at home against Rangers, where this can also come to life again. But that is far away.

“First things first, Saturday lies another challenge.”.

Reedijk was also pleased to see Cadden rack up a stunning strike – the wing-back finding the net in only his second start of the season.

The effort came from a cleverly worked corner routine, with Hibs having already threatened from a similar set-piece earlier in the match.

Reedijk also singled out assistant coach Rogier Molhoek for praise for devising the short corner routines.

According to recent reports, he added: “It was a beautiful goal, wasn’t it? It was one when he left the foot, I was like, ‘ooh, he hits it well and you saw the angle of the ball’.

“We try to use every quality we have in order to make it difficult for opponents to see what we are doing in the beginning. Also we look at their organisation and if their organisation allows us to attack certain spaces, we try to do this.

“This is the job of Rogier, he always makes routines – and also with crazy names. You will never know these names because sometimes it’s not polite.”.

Dundee boss Steven Pressley was encouraged by his side’s response to the humiliation against Hearts despite his team falling to a third consecutive league loss.

He said: “Both teams are a bit fragile and there was a lot of trepidation in the game but the one thing about us we got a degree of pride back. It’s not the result but a little bit of stability and we highlighted a lot of courage.

“We wanted to give ourselves a foundation to build from and we gave ourselves that.

“We were much more cohesive in the second half and when you suffer the defeat we suffered on Saturday and you come here and you find yourself 2-0 down at half-time, it asks a lot of questions of you as a group and I thought they responded brilliantly.

“They demonstrated courage and spirit and it’s not been easy because there’s a fragility about us. We responded in the proper manner.”.

‘Thank goodness neither team lost’ – Enfield Town and Eastbourne Borough serve up match-of-season contender

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight goals were shared in a crazy 4-4 contest that lurched in all directions, the Isthmian Premier points shared, a proper sporting contest in the best traditions of non-league football.
  • Recent findings suggest that old men have long memories.
  • Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight goals were shared in a crazy 4-4 contest that lurched in all directions, the Isthmian Premier points shared, a proper sporting contest in the best traditions of non-league football.

Recent findings suggest that old men have long memories. Well before kick-off, sitting up in Enfield's distinctive Art Deco grandstand, I fell into conversation with an octogenarian - 83 to be exact, as he proudly told me - who had travelled up to this fixture from his Littlehampton home. But he was born and raised in North London, and he proudly recounted his Wembley trips for FA Amateur Cup finals with the old Enfield FC.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Ah yes, chipped in your Herald reporter, 1966 against Skelmersdale - I too was there, on a Wembley day out with my own football-daft dad! And if that anecdote is worth a column inch, it is because non-league football ripples with such memories.

In a recent development, down below us, the teams had done their warm-up routines, taken in all the instructions, and - to a guard of honour from the local primary school - were filing out for a crucial Isthmian Premier contest. Second versus third; valuable points to play for.

Recent findings suggest that borough flew out of the traps, and after a couple of Freddie Carter long throws had ruffled the home defence, they were ahead on seven minutes. Terrell Egbri, a turbo-charged winger all afternoon, cut in from the right to whip in a cross - or was it a shot? Either way, the ball spun wickedly in off the woodwork past helpless home keeper Thompson.

Both sides were energised, and play swung end to end with a glorious lack of caution and Thomas Avgoustidis levelled for Town.

The Sports looked stronger, swarming all over the home defence, and Liam Nash flicked a back-header just over, then the industrious Max Sheaf combined with Nash for a fizzing low ball across the Enflied goalmouth - but nobody managed a touch.

Steve King's side were not to be denied. Sam Oguntayo - nominally a full-back but so often a marauding extra attacker - swung over a cross which Thompson pushed over for a Borough corner, recycled and whacked goalwards by Sheaf. With Enfield throwing bodies into the mix, the unfortunate Tommy Avgoustidis back-headed into his own net for a 2-1 Borough lead.

It is axiomatic among coaches that you need to score when your side is on top - even with a lead. When King and his staff looked back on the 15 minutes to half-time, they will have noted five or six chances to have put this game to bed – though credit goes to home keeper Thompson for some alert stops and one brilliant save to deny Darren McQueen.

But the start of the second half saw a huge momentum swing: Enfield introduced Orient loanee Tariq Al Sadee - fresh from international action with Oman - and the home side had reclaimed the midfield initiative. An excellent Lewis Carey save denied Avgoustidis and then Oguntayo cleared off the line from one of four home corners.

And just as King was reinforcing his midfield with Craig Eastmond off the bench, the Towners seized an equaliser, Luke May-Parrott streaking away to beat Carey. 2-2, and half-hour of mayhem, magic and madness to come.

It has been revealed that for a while, Borough were reeling. Tariq was striding everywhere and Enfield were revitalised. On 63 minutes, a pass through the right flank sliced open the Sports, and Luke May-Parrott's low angled shot put the home side ahead for the first time.

It has been revealed that mcQueen almost restored parity but put his shot just wide. And with the Sports pressing high and possibly a tiny bit overstretched, a long clearance out of the Enfield defence allowed Avgoustidis to pound through open space and strike an effort which Carey should really have stopped, but it squirmed over the line for 4-2.

In a recent development, at this point routine, sensible football matches peter out, as winning sides shut down, losing sides struggle for openings and chances, everything goes to script, and everybody consigns the result to history. Fortunately, King prefers his teams to write their own scripts. With Kai Corbett and Tyano Wilson bringing fresh impetus off the bench, Borough were energised again.

Wilson was getting possession in dangerous areas, and he squirmed in from the left to drill a lethal low ball across the goalmouth. Corbett pounced from close range, and the match was alive again at 4-3.

And with the Towners showing no real signs, or capacity, to shut down the match, we had a brilliant climax to relish. The Sports were chasing down everything, and Enfield were flapping.

That final goal just had to be Borough's. With seven minutes to play, Kai Corbett was released from halfway to tear into the Enfield defence. Cutting in from the right, he chose to shoot early and rocketed his low shot into the right hand corner of the home net.

Eight goals shared, the points shared, and an engrossing, exhausting non-league football match shared. Football should always be like this.

You can pay much, much more for a seat in a splendid Premier League stadium - albeit segregated and strictly policed - and you might even see an eight-goal thriller. But up in Enfield Town's quirky main stand, as spectators shook hands all around, one home supporter summed it up perfectly: "Thank goodness neither side lost!".

Derek McInnes has warned his Rangers side they must learn to control games more efficiently for longer periods if they are to sustain their Scottish Premiership title challenge this season.

The Ibrox manager praised the resilience of his players after they managed to overturn a half-time deficit to beat a revitalised Aberdeen 3-2 in a thrilling contest, courtesy of a decisive ten-minute goal blitz early in the second half.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, McInnes was frustrated that Rangers allowed their opponents back swiftly into the contest after establishing a seemingly unassailable cushion, which left them clinging on during an increasingly anxious finale.

Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin turned the game around, before Findlay Marshall's immediate response ensured the Dons went down fighting.

Despite the satisfaction of extending their unbeaten run to 14 matches, McInnes was unhappy with the manner in which his team surrendered control, insisting his players put unnecessary pressure on themselves.

According to recent reports, “Delighted we've got the job done. Great win for us in the end,” he said. “Disappointed we've allowed ourselves to be hanging on at the end rather than controlling the game. The question was being asked of us at half-time. We were in a difficult spot. We were having to dig it deep and you find out about your players in these sort of situations. It's good to know that we have dug that result out.

Recent findings suggest that “We need to recognise that we need to be better for longer periods, particularly at Ibrox. By conceding the second goal, we should still stay on the job, but with too many negative passes, too many backwards passes, we need to own that a wee bit.

"The biggest takeaway for me tonight is my players had to dig deep. We were in a tough spot at half-time, 50,000, 1-0 down at home to Aberdeen. That's not an easy place to be. It's alright for me to try and address it tactically, having a go at half-time or whatever, but they've still got to go and deliver, and they delivered a major performance.”.

According to recent reports, mcInnes had initially opted for a system designed to exploit the spaces around Aberdeen's front two, with Gassama and Badredine Bouanani providing width on both flanks. However, he conceded that his side had not been productive enough despite repeatedly getting into promising positions in the final third before a triple half-time substitution altered the formation to provide greater control in central areas.

In a recent development, “I thought the subs helped us and I thought for 20 minutes we were outstanding,” McInnes added. “We highlighted the speed, the intensity, the quality, the intelligence. We blew them away.”.

Upcoming Aberdeen head coach Mario Frick was left frustrated by his side’s collapse immediately after half-time, but felt they had shown enough to suggest Rangers were there for the taking.

Industry observers note that “I am disappointed with the five or six minutes after half-time. That hurts,” he stated. “We saw a good performance, Rangers were beatable tonight. We need more time. We have to improve. We have to talk about those ten minutes.

Sources indicate that “After 3-1 down we came back and we believed in ourselves. We deserved the equaliser. We came to win and we are disappointed to go back with zero points. I see a lot of positives things.”.

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

In a recent development, the giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

Recent findings suggest that if you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”.

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

It has been revealed that as Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”.

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

Sources indicate that they travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are at the moment third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

By Carter White | 23 Nov 2026 17:51.

Still searching for that elusive home league victory, Burnley welcome Birmingham City to Turf Moor for a Championship battle on Wednesday night.

The Clarets shared the spoils in the East Lancashire derby against Blackburn Rovers on the weekend, whilst Blues were bested in a top-of-the-table clash by Stoke City in Staffordshire.

Burnley's winless run in the Championship extended to seven matches (D3 L4) due to a 2-2 draw with rivals Blackburn on Sunday afternoon, after which defender Kyle Walker conceded that his side were in a relegation battle.

Goals either side of the half-time whistle from Largie Ramazani and Jaydon Banel were not enough to claim maximum points at the expense of Rovers, with the Clarets last winning a home league fixture in October 2025.

Winning just one of their opening 16 second-tier fixtures of the campaign, Burnley are at the moment occupying 22nd position in the Championship rankings, four points from the safety of managerless Watford in 21st place.

As alluded to earlier, the Clarets are the only side in the division who are yet to enjoy a victory in front of their home faithful, with Wednesday's hosts drawing six and losing two of their eight Turf Moor clashes.

The October arrival of Swiss manager Fabio Celestini to replace Nicky Hayen has failed to get Burnley on the winning track, with the 51-year-old enduring a four-game winless run (D3 L1) at the beginning of his Lancashire tenure.

Following three straight consecutive Championship wins, Birmingham City spent the November international break at the very summit of the second-tier rankings, however, Saturday's defeat by Stoke knocked Chris Davies's side off their perch.

In the end, a second-half strike from former Ipswich Town marksman George Hirst was enough to beat Blues, who failed to take advantage of a numerical advantage after Luca Bombino's 63rd-minute dismissal.

Despite the weekend's loss at the bet365 Stadium, Birmingham have made an exceptional start to the 2026-27 campaign and sit in fourth place in the Championship standings, three points behind league leaders Middlesbrough.

Davies's troops are much-improved on their travels compared to last term, however, the Second City club have lost two of their past three away contests, including a trip to Cardiff City (0-1) in October.

Given Burnley's success in the Championship over the past decade or so, it is no surprise that Birmingham are six games without a win in this matchup (W3 D3), last defeating the Clarets at Turf Moor in January 2013, when Marlon King netted a 90th-minute winner.

Birmingham City Championship form:.

Picking up a straight red card in the 5-4 defeat by Cardiff at the start of the month, Burnley's Connor Roberts remains unavailable this week.

The Clarets have a number of attacking options on the sidelines, including Armando Broja, Ashley Barnes and Dastan Satpaev.

Birmingham are sweating over the fitness of Jhon Solis, with the Colombia international missing the loss at Stoke on Saturday.

The former Girona man would be a major miss at Turf Moor, where Blues might field Paik Seung-Ho alongside Tomoki Iwata in the midfield once again.

Collecting his fifth yellow card of the season last time out, captain Christoph Klarer is suspended and should be replaced by Dael Fry at centre-back.

Burnley possible starting lineup:.

Weiss; Walker, Alleyne, Julio, Sonne; Hatate, Cullen, Laurent; Ramazani, Edwards, Amdouni.

Birmingham City possible starting lineup:.

Allsop; Osayi-Samuel, Neumann, Fry, Cochrane; Iwata, Paik; Vicente, Stansfield, Millar; Priske.

Without a home league victory in over 13 months, Burnley are low on confidence despite a recent managerial alteration.

Birmingham are not the same beast without Solis but should be good enough for at least a point at Turf Moor.
